strings.text: Moominpappa at Sea

The end of August: everything in the valley is done, and Moominpappa takes his family to a bare island with a dark lighthouse. Each of them looks for a place of their own there — and each finds a loneliness. Whom does Papa notice, and whom does he miss?
A bare island, a dark lighthouse, one lantern for the whole family — and whom will Papa give it to?
after the novel by Tove Jansson
The Crossing
The lantern in the boat
Put it out
Leave it burning
Give it to the son
The Fisherman
“We are the new keepers”
Ask him to breakfast
Sit beside him in silence
In truth: the open sea at night; the boat Adventure under the stars, the lantern on her bow.
We steer by that star. The captain knows the way
Mama is asleep under a blanket; Little My sits up the mast. In the stern Moomintroll sees a white strip of frost on the water behind them — and in it, two eyes.
He pulls his paws in from the gunwale and edges up against sleeping Mama, close. He looks at the grown-ups — and says nothing. Then he turns to look back again.
Silence. The boat under the stars, only the water. The boy keeps looking back.
In truth: the open sea at night, the boat Adventure.
Papa sees where his son is looking and glances round: a white strip on the water.
The moon’s path. Pretty
The eyes he does not see: he has to look ahead.
“Put out the lantern. We’ll go by the stars.”
“Leave it burning. Mama will wake up and be frightened.”
“Here. Shine it back, since you’re looking.”
Put out the lantern. We’ll go by the stars
The boat goes on by moonlight; the strip falls behind and is gone. Mama wakes up in the dark.
Where are we?
Where we ought to be
She does not sleep till morning; on the island she falls asleep sitting up, on the bundle of blankets.
Leave it burning. Mama will wake up and be frightened
Papa tucks the blanket round Mama. The strip comes nearer; now the boy sees the eyes clearly, presses into sleeping Mama, his paws on the gunwale shaking. Papa looks ahead and does not see it.
Here. Shine it back, since you’re looking
Papa gives the lantern to his son. The boy, shaking, holds the beam on the Groke with both paws — she follows the light behind the stern. Papa steers without a light:
So… a bit to the left… I think

The boat drifts. Frost creeps along the stern to the boy, his paws on the lantern turn white, and he does not let go. At dawn Mama sees his paws, throws off her blanket and rubs them; he goes ashore wrapped in her blanket.
23 August. Bare pink rocks, a white lighthouse, wind. The door is locked.
A keeper always leaves the key. That’s how it’s done
Little My is already sitting by a stone with an arrow scratched on it.
There’s an arrow here. For fools
The key is under the stone.
On the rocks by the landing — a white patch.
Somebody has been here
Gulls
Papa carries in the can of paraffin.
Enough for three lanterns
Papa looks out of the window at the white crests.
When the wind drops I’ll sail for more. This is going to be our home
The walls are written over in pencil.
Wind south-west. Nobody again
She roars with laughter. Under the line, a knot of fishing net — the eye stays on it a moment.
Papa writes his log on the wall, right over “Nobody again”: “23 August. Arrived.”
You’ve covered him up
He doesn’t need it any more
Papa writes standing, high up. Mama, crouching by the basket with her back to him, finds a place on the windowsill and paints the first stalk there.
Papa walks round “his” island and comes out on the cape behind a stranger’s back: a man with a net on his knees, sitting side-on to the lighthouse. He does not turn round.
“We are the new keepers. If anything happens — you know where to find us.”
“We have breakfast by the lighthouse. Do come.”
Sit down beside him without a word
We are the new keepers. If anything happens — you know where to find us
At the word “keepers” the Fisherman turns his head — and turns away. Papa leaves pleased; the Fisherman watches his back, then the lighthouse.
We have breakfast by the lighthouse. Do come
No need
Mamma bakes pancakes…
The Fisherman gets up with his net and goes off further over the rocks. Papa stands alone: he forced himself on him. From that day Mama leaves bread for him on a stone.
A long pause. The wind.
The sea is good today
Good
They sit. By the lighthouse Mama hauls the wet bundles up the steps alone; one slips into the water, she fishes it out, wet to the elbows.
When Papa comes back everything is in. She is sitting on a step, wringing out her sleeve.
All done
In truth: the lantern room at the top of the lighthouse.
In truth: the shore at night; the Groke by the water.
The Lighthouse Is Dark
Papa’s day
Measure the pool
Carry seaweed for Mama
Go to the Fisherman
Whose lantern tonight
Up to the lamp
Mama, with a term
The son, no questions
By turns

The same day, afternoon. Cloudy lenses, a barrel of oil: Papa dips a finger in — it is thick as jam and will not run. The wall by the burner is black with soot; under the soot, pencil — by day only grooves under the finger.
The flame catches, smokes and goes out.
He doesn’t want to
Little My, from below, through the hatch:
It’s you who can’t
A lighthouse takes time!
In truth: the island — the shore, the pines in the middle of it, a clearing.
Mama takes her basket down to the water for seaweed — on bare stone she needs earth — and for driftwood for the stove.
On her way she leaves bread on a stone by the cape.
Little My goes off over the rocks. Without Papa, you see Moomintroll find a clearing among the pines and set stones in a ring.
Mine
By the water, the sea horses. He crouches down:
How beautiful you are…
The sea horses laugh and swim away. He turns red.
In truth: the island, the same afternoon.
Measure the black pool
Go to the Fisherman and ask about the lighthouse
In truth: the middle of the island, the black pool.
A rope with a weight on it.
There is no bottom. In the log: “Depth: more than the rope.” Papa is happy and puzzled; behind his back the pines have shifted toward the lighthouse.
In the evening Mama comes back wet, with an empty basket: the seaweed was washed away.
In truth: the shore and the pines in the middle of the island.

He cannot see his feet under the armful: Papa goes straight through the pines and knocks down his son’s ring of stones. The boy stands at the edge of the clearing looking at his back; when Papa has gone he sets the stones back, one by one.
At the landing Papa and Mama lay the seaweed into a cleft together.
Nothing will grow here
It will for me
She laughs.
Papa sits down as he did the first time. The Fisherman’s net is in a tangle.
Papa untangles it without a word; the Fisherman looks at his paws on his net — and does not take it away.
Why isn’t he lit?
The Fisherman looks at the sea for a long time.
He shines outward
The Fisherman sees someone coming, gets up and goes off over the rocks; his net, spread out to dry, has caught on a stone and stayed behind. Papa sits down by the net.
The Fisherman comes back quickly, takes the net out of his paws without a word and goes; he does not look at Papa. Papa is left empty-handed on a stranger’s stone.
Papa notices: the knot on the net is the same as the one under the lines on the wall.
In the evening Mama comes back wet, with an empty basket.
In truth: a rock facing the sea, at dusk.
Papa alone on a rock, facing the sea. He says nothing, only looks.
I’ll understand you. You’ll see
A wave splashes over his boots.
On the windowsill there is still only the one stalk from the first day, and fresh paint on the brush.
Mama paints on the windowsill: {n} flower so far.
strings.plural: Mama paints on the windowsill: {n} flowers so far.

strings.text: In her own paints: the flowers are green.
In red lead for boats and blue paint for window frames from the storeroom: the flowers come out red and blue, not hers.
The bread was taken
By evening the stove is cold, the driftwood all used (in the morning Mama will gather more). The lantern burns on the table. In the can: three measures.
At dusk frost whitens by the water: a strip of it from the sea — she came to the light in the window. The Groke sits down on the sand facing the lighthouse.
At dusk frost whitens by the water: the Groke sits down on the sand facing the lighthouse — nearer than one would think.
At dusk frost whitens by the water: the Groke sits down on the sand facing the lighthouse.
A lighthouse is lit at dusk
He looks at the hatch.
So light it, then
Mama sews, pulled right up to the lantern, squinting at the needle. At once she pushes the lantern over to Papa:
Take it, take it. I can see well enough
She sews on, squinting. Papa moves the lantern back; without raising her eyes she pushes it to him again:
Take it, take it
Moomintroll, looking out of the window:
Can I have the lantern? For the whole night
What for?
I need it
He will not say more. My looks at her brother and smirks. The lantern in the middle of the table; Mama and the boy near it, Papa by the stair. Everyone looks at the lantern, nobody at each other.

Night 1, 23/24 August. Papa fills the lantern — one measure, till morning. There is no other light: the candles stayed in the valley, the stove is lit once a day, the lighthouse is dark, and no sailing for paraffin while the crests are white.
Up to the lamp: “Till I light it, I sleep by the lamp.”
To Mama: “The captain sets a term. Not lit by the full moon — we turn for home.”
To the son: “Take it. I won’t ask.”
By turns: “Mama till bedtime, then me, toward morning — you.”
Till I light it, I sleep by the lamp
He carries the lantern away. The room in moonlight; Mama puts down her sewing. The boy at the window.
In the slanting light the grooves under the soot come up. Papa reads:
“In wind, warm the burner with paraffin till the flame turns blue. Do not let go before.”
At once he splashes paraffin from the lantern on the burner and strikes a match: the flame turns blue and goes out — the thick oil will not come.
He pins a sheet up by the lamp — the sheet “Burner” — and sets up a camp bed. On the shore the Groke looks up at the far little light in the lantern room; she does not come, and she howls.
The captain sets a term. If it isn’t lit by the full moon — we turn for home
Mama looks at him for a long time.
Three nights till the full moon
Three
Home? Where everything’s done?
Without a word Mama moves along the bench, making room. He sits down. The boy at the window; outside, the Groke howls.
Somebody is crying
Lying down, she turns the wick low but does not put it out:
Let it burn low
Take it. I won’t ask
He takes it without surprise.
First he looks at his father, not believing it.
He goes out without raising his eyes. Mama looks Papa in the face and says nothing, only puts down her sewing. Papa goes up and sits by the cold lamp, listening.
What Papa does not see: on the shore the boy sets the lantern on a stone —
There. That’s for you
— and backs away three steps as the Groke rises. She sways over the light, clumsy and quiet, as if dancing.
At dawn the boy brings the lantern back with its last flicker and sets it on the floor by his bunk. Papa comes down, and in the low slanting light, right by the floor, he sees a line:
“27 August. Wind north. I am forty today. Nobody knows.” Under it, a knot. The flicker goes out.
Mama till bedtime, then me, and toward morning — you
Papa turns the wick down, so there will be enough for everyone. Mama sews by the low flame and pricks her finger; when Papa gets up by the stair, she lays her sewing down in the middle of a seam:
All right
When he has gone up she moves to the window and finishes the seam by moonlight.
Toward morning Papa sets the lantern on the middle step of the stair. The boy has waited below without sleeping; he runs to the shore.
The Groke is already up to her waist in the water; she turns to the dim light, comes out and sits down at the water’s edge, far off, till dawn.
In the morning the lantern stands on the middle step again, in frost. Papa shakes it — empty, as after a full flame.
Mama’s Garden
Mama in the wall
“She’s out walking” — and up
Call her
A cup, and wait
Night 2: the hand on the lantern
Don’t open your eyes
“Put it back”
Go after him
24 August. The door will not open: in the night the pines have crept up to the very threshold.
Trees don’t walk
They’re afraid
On the stone by the threshold, tracks of frost — from the shore to the door and back. Far off the Fisherman is walking away from the lighthouse: at dawn he was here.
The boy at the table, his paws white with cold. Without the lantern he sat by the Groke in the night, far from her — his first small step.
The boy at the table, his paws white with cold: he sat by the light on the wet sand.
Mama drops the cup she was washing, takes his paws in hers without a word and rubs them. She asks nothing. Papa looks at the tracks and at the paws.
Toughening up. Quite right
My looks at her brother.
Papa says nothing. For a moment the boy lifts his eyes to him.
Papa says nothing and looks at the lantern in frost on the middle step.
On the wall, overnight, a garden has grown: an apple tree, a veranda, a stream. Painted in it: the boy, My, Mama with her basket.
Mama had no lantern: she painted by moonlight. The brush lies on the sill in the square of moonlight, the paint still fresh.
By the gate stands a little Papa.
Ti-iny, isn’t it
And no Papa
He’s at the lighthouse
Noon. Papa is up top, rubbing the lenses. My is on the windowsill outside, the boy in the pines. Quiet.
Mama rubs her eyes and sits down, the way one sits down to rest.
Mama looks round at the empty room.

She finishes the last branch, steps back, looks — and steps into the wall, under the apple tree. Her little figure sits down in the grass. Instead of the wind — the garden, bees. You and My see it through the glass; Papa does not.
Papa comes down. The table, cold tea, wind in the chimney. Mama is not there.
My looks in at the door and at the wall:
That’s new. Wasn’t there this morning
Fine

Papa looks at the wall: under the apple tree, a little figure that was not there in the morning — an apron, a handbag. He knows her. He lays his palm on the painted gate: under his paw, plaster. He cannot get in there. His face, close.
“She’s out walking. The island is small” — and up to the lamp
Call: “Mamma! Mamma!” — his palm on the wall
Put a cup of tea by the wall and sit down to wait. Not to move, whoever comes
She’s out walking. The island is small
Papa at the lamp till dusk: he rubs the lenses, strikes matches, talks to the burner. And here, all day, the wall: Mama’s figure under the apple tree, the bees.
At dusk, when the room is empty, Mama comes out of the wall. Only My sees it, from the windowsill.
Mamma! Mamma!
Mama comes out at once, embarrassed and tired.
I only lay down for a moment under the apple tree
She stays with him till evening. Her brushes she puts away in a jar and does not touch them again; the apple tree is left without its last leaves.
Two more nights
The light in the window goes from noon toward dusk; the tea goes cold, Papa pours fresh. Around Mama’s figure on the wall, all day, flowers add themselves.
He knows the line of 27 August already; he reads the next one: “Ate bread. Whose — don’t know.”
“27 August. Wind north. I am forty today. Nobody knows.” And under it, a knot.
In the afternoon the boy in the doorway, a stone from his ring in his paws. For the first time his father sits on the floor, low, the way he sits himself; the boy looks a long time — and comes in:
Pappa, I…
Papa, not turning from the wall, lifts a paw:
Shh. Later
The boy turns red and goes. The stone stays on the threshold.
At dusk Mama comes out by herself, sees the cup, touches it — a knock against the table — and says nothing. She sits down beside him on the floor.
And I found a line here, by the way. The old keeper’s. By myself, under the dust
And he waits.
How good that you noticed
Night 2, 24/25 August. One measure of paraffin left. The moon almost full. The Groke by the rocks — right up against them.
Night 2, 24/25 August. One measure of paraffin left. The moon almost full. The Groke by the rocks.

Papa carries the lantern up and falls asleep over the lamp; the lantern stands on the floor, its light falls on the soot straight on, and the grooves do not show. Below it is dark; Mama lies awake facing the wall and hums softly, like the bees in her garden; the howling she seems not to hear.
In the night the boy appears in the hatch and reaches for the lantern.
In truth: the lantern room, night.
Mama sat on at the table with Papa and fell asleep on the bench in the middle of a word; Papa turns the wick down himself. The boy comes to the table.
Papa has dozed off on the floor by the cup. Mama, going to bed, turns the wick down:
Let it burn low. Somebody’s howling
The boy comes to the table.
Papa wakes at a creak and sees his son’s hand on the lantern.
Up top the camp bed is empty: “I sleep by the lamp” is broken.
“Where are you going? Put it back. I need it.”
The boy goes.
The Groke sways over the light — the second time, and nearer. The frost under her is less.
The Groke sways over the light. The frost under her is less.
Where are you going? Put it back. I need it
The boy sets the lantern down without looking and stands at the window till dawn.
Papa turns the wick up, holds the lantern sideways to the soot and reads the next piece:
The sheet “Burner”.
“The oil is thick: warm it in a pan on the stove, carry it wrapped. On a quiet evening the warm oil runs by itself; in wind — only with paraffin.”
The sheet “Pan”.
Papa lies awake, looking at his son’s back by the window.
“I won’t ask” is broken.
The boy sets the lantern on a stone; the Groke rises toward the light. Papa stops on the dune. The boy knows he is there and does not turn round.
Up top the camp bed stays empty till morning: “I sleep by the lamp” is broken.
In the morning:
You promised not to ask
I didn’t ask
Spy
In truth: the lantern room and its glass gallery, in the storm.
Papa goes. Mama says nothing after him; later, to the wall:
Well, there
Papa goes. Mama, after him:
Be careful out there
The Storm
Where Papa is in the storm
Light the lighthouse
Hold the door with everyone
To the Fisherman on the cape
The burner — and run down
Night 3: the paw on his shoulder
“Let him go”
“Mama is right”
“As far as the dune”
25 August, grey, the wind getting up; tonight is the full moon.
There’s going to be a storm
Papa and his son pull the boat higher up the rocks. The boy pulls from the other side of the hull, without a word.
Papa and his son pull the boat higher up the rocks. The boy pulls beside him, without a word.
Breakfast. Papa tells how he pulled up the boat.
With one paw, you might say. Against the wind
He pulled too
Your son takes the lantern to the Groke. Every night
Your son took the lantern to the Groke. The one you left him
Your son took the lantern to the Groke last night. And you snored. Pretending
Your son goes to the Groke at night. Without a lantern. He sits there and freezes
The boy gets up and leaves the table. Mama heard it.
Mama knows where the boy goes at night.
Mama was in the wall all day yesterday. She came out when you weren’t there
My
And nothing more.
My says nothing and smirks.

Toward evening, the wind already howling, Papa lights the stove — the only time today — with the whole bundle of driftwood, but not for supper: he warms a pan of oil, wraps it in his coat and carries it up to the lamp.
Supper is cold bread.
Bread again
By evening, the storm. The wind; a wave washes over the landing and reaches the boat even up on the rocks. A wave comes down the chimney and floods the stove — hissing, steam.
The stove’s flooded

The door will not stay shut by itself. Up top the glass of the gallery rings: up there, by the lamp, there is no room for everyone. Through the window — the cape: the Fisherman sits, a wave runs in under him, and he does not get up. The last measure in the can. The full moon in a rift of cloud.
Mama ties the shutters, then stands silent beside Papa, holding on to his sleeve.
Mama ties the shutters without a word.
Mama ties the shutters and for a moment lays her palm on the painted gate.
The first thing she saves from the water is her box of paints; she holds it under her apron.
She looks out at the moon:
Full moon
Light the lighthouse with the last of the paraffin
Hold the door with everyone: “When it drops, we sail home.”
Go out to the cape, to the Fisherman
Light the burner — and run down to the door
The last measure goes. The can is empty.
Papa on the gallery shouts into the storm, as at an enemy:
You won’t take it! Do you hear? You won’t take it!
The sea answers with a wave against the glass.
By the lamp: two sheets, and the pan of warm oil.
The oil is warm. Till it turns blue
By the lamp: one sheet, “Burner”. No pan.
Till it turns blue
By the lamp: no sheets, no pan.
Well. Come on

The warm oil runs up the wick, the flame rises, the lenses turn, the beam goes out over the storm and over the cape. Under the wave the Fisherman lifts his face to the light. Papa on the gallery, soaked, laughing.
The paraffin burns blue, the thick oil will not come; the flame rises and goes out. Lightning — Papa’s face, close. He listens to the wind by the cold lamp.
Below, Mama alone with the children holds the door.
The last of the paraffin goes into the lantern on the table. Papa says it loudly, like an order on board, his back to the hatch:
When it drops, we sail home
The captain remembers
The four of them sit with their backs against the door. Papa tells about the storm at the Lonely Mountains.
You’ve told that one
They laugh.
Mama says it to the painted apple tree, under her breath, under the blow of a wave; Papa at the door does not hear, you do:
I want to go home
Mama, to Papa — not asking, owning up:
Pass me the blanket
In a flash of lightning through the window: the lighthouse without a light, and someone on the cape under the wave.
Man overboard. The captain is going
Have you gone mad?
Where are you going, in such water?
The last of the paraffin goes into the lantern.
In truth: the cape in the storm, at night.
Halfway there the lantern blows out. Papa shouts at the sea:
You won’t get me!

The moon in a rift of cloud, foam. Papa takes the Fisherman by the sleeve and pulls him toward the rock; the Fisherman does not move, does not even look. Papa lets go of the sleeve and sits down beside him, under the same wave. He shouts at the sea no more: the wave covers them both and goes back, and Papa listens to it breathe.
Lightning: both faces, close. On the Fisherman’s knees the net — and the knot, close: the same as under the lines on the wall.
The Fisherman looks at the dark lighthouse:
On a night like this he ought to burn
His palm comes down on his knee and presses, the way one holds a burner — and lets go. Papa looks at his hand.
The Fisherman spoke to Papa.
The Fisherman is silent till dawn, and Papa understands only that he will not leave.
Below, Mama, My and the boy hold the door, the three of them, without warm light.
The flame goes out behind his back.
Below, the wave has already come in: the floor is wet, Mama and the children are at the door. He stands with them, but the door is already held.
26 August. The storm has dropped; for the first time, no wind. In the room it drips from the ceiling; the can is empty; the stove is flooded.
The lamp burnt out at dawn: the warm oil ran out.
Mama packs her basket without a word and sets it by the door.
Papa does not go down to the water.
Papa goes down to the water: the sea is smooth and splashes over his boots, as it did that dusk, and the whole shore at his feet is driftwood it threw up in the night.
There, you see
He says nothing.
He crouches down and runs his paw over the water:
There, there. It’s all right
He looks at the sea over his shoulder and goes to the boat.
The boat has a crack in her side. All day Papa caulks her; the tar will be dry by morning — no sailing to the neighbours for paraffin, and no sailing home.

Night 3, 26/27 August, quiet. No paraffin, the lantern empty, the lamp cold, nothing to warm it with. On the shore the Groke, the frost around her wide; she sits nearer the lighthouse than ever. She howls.
Night 3, 26/27 August, quiet. No paraffin, the lantern empty, the lamp cold, nothing to warm it with. On the shore the Groke, the frost around her wide. She howls.
The boy at the door, without a lantern. He does not look at Papa.
The boy at the door, without a lantern. First he looks at Papa, then at the door.
The boy at the door, without a lantern.
The stone from the threshold is in his paws. Papa opens his mouth —
Later
— the boy says without looking, and grips the stone.
Without a lantern? She’ll freeze you
Let her
Where are you going? To freeze again?
I need to
Tell him
Papa’s paw is on his son’s shoulder.
“Let him go.”
“Mama is right.”
“Come on. I’ll go with you as far as the dune.”
Let him go

The boy sits down beside the Groke. The frost creeps toward him; he sits a long time, white to the elbows. Mama takes a blanket without a word, goes to the dune, lays it on the sand behind the boy’s back and comes back; till morning she stands at the window, Papa behind her.
By the middle of the night the frost stops; the sand under the Groke darkens; she hums softly.
At dawn the boy, in the blanket, looking at no one, says in the doorway:
She isn’t frightening. She’s just cold
Mama rubs his paws and sits down beside him; Papa she gives tea, and does not sit down by him.
Mama is right
He trembles in the doorway and obeys, but after that he does not look at Papa.
The boy at the window till dawn. The Groke howls, and toward morning she goes off into the sea; on the sand, a white track into the water. Mama covers the boy with a blanket.
Come on. I’ll go with you as far as the dune
I’ll go on by myself from here
Papa sits on the dune all night. The Groke sees a second figure and for a long time does not come; the frost reaches the boy. Only toward dawn does she sit down beside him, and the sand darkens.
In the room Mama puts two cups on the table; one goes cold. At dawn the boy walks past Papa and does not stop.
Epilogue
27 August: the second quiet day. The boat is tarred, the driftwood on the rocks has dried, the stove has dried out.
The wall: Mama’s garden in green, her own paints.
The wall: Mama’s garden in red and blue — red lead and window paint, not hers.
The garden is unfinished; by the gate, a little Papa.
So much of the garden is painted: {n} of 4.
At some moment Mama is in the garden again: a figure under the apple tree, the table empty.
The brushes dry in a jar, the apple tree without leaves; Mama at the table.
Two cups on the table.
The line of 27 August by the floor, wiped clean.
The line of 27 August by the floor, under dust.
The stone with the arrow.
The cleft by the landing: a green sprout.
The cleft by the landing: bare.
The rock by the pool: the coiled rope, and in the log, “Depth: more than the rope.”
The cape: the Fisherman turns away.
The cape: the Fisherman lifts a hand.
The cape: the Fisherman looks Papa’s way.
His net is spread out, and Papa sees the place he untangled.
Catching Papa’s look, the Fisherman rolls up his net.
The shore: dark sand under the Groke, the boy beside her.
The shore: a white track into the water; the boy alone, looking at the sea.
The shore: the boy by the Groke; he walks past Papa.
Less frost: she was given light.
The boy does not look at Papa once.
Once, the boy turns to look at Papa.
The boy looks at the sea.
The camp bed up top is slept in: the promise kept.
The camp bed up top is empty: the promise broken.
Mama’s basket, packed, by the door: the term was not kept.
The stone in the boy’s paws; the ring in the clearing is one stone short.
What the camera passes
In truth: the lighthouse, lit; the lantern room and the room below.
The Beam
In the first shot Mama unpacks her basket without a word.
The lighthouse is lit. It caught in the storm, and from the 27th it burns every night: on quiet days the warm oil runs by itself, and by the first wind Papa has brought a new can on the mended boat.
A week later. Papa sailed for paraffin and for a week learnt the lamp by himself, till the oil ran.
I can now
All week Papa sleeps up top; every evening Mama puts his cup on the table, and by morning it is full.
Papa on the gallery is writing the Big Book about the Sea.
The beam passes Mama: the table empty, she is under the apple tree on the wall.
The beam passes Mama: at the table, by the leafless apple tree.
The beam passes Mama: at the table, by two cups.
My on a rock. The Fisherman on the cape.
The shore: empty sand and a white track into the water; the boy alone by the water.
The shore: the boy on dark sand by the Groke. The Groke reaches toward the beam, and it goes on.
My lies on her stomach by the wall and reads the lowest lines, the way she read them all:
